content: Ras-related protein Ral-B (RalB) is a protein encoded by the RALB gene located on chromosome 2 in humans. It belongs to the Ras GTPase family and is one of two paralogs of the Ral protein, the other being RalA. RalA and RalB act as molecular switches that regulate various biological processes, primarily cell division and intracellular transport, through signaling pathways. Due to its role in these processes, RalB is implicated in the development and progression of several cancers. Structure RalA and RalB share approximately 80% similarity in their overall amino acid sequences and are identical in their effector-binding regions. However, they differ significantly in their C-terminal hypervariable regions, which contain multiple sites for post-translational modifications. These modifications influence their subcellular localization and biological functions. For instance, phosphorylation of serine 194 on RalA by the kinase Aurora A causes RalA to relocate to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it facilitates mitochondrial fission. In contrast, phosphorylation of serine 198 on RalB by protein kinase C (PKC) leads to its relocation to other internal membranes and activates its tumorigenic functions. Function RalB is a member of the Ral family, which is a subfamily of the Ras family of small GTPases. Like other Ras GTPases, RalB functions as a molecular switch, becoming active when bound to GTP and inactive when bound to GDP. RalB is activated by Ral guanine nucleotide exchange factors (RalGEFs) and, in turn, activates downstream effectors in signaling pathways to mediate various biological processes. RalB interacts with components of the exocyst complex, such as Exo84 and Sec5, to regulate processes like autophagosome assembly, secretory vesicle trafficking, and vesicle tethering. Other biological functions of RalB include exocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis, tight junction formation, filopodia formation, mitochondrial fission, and cytokinesis. While many of these functions are shared with RalA, the distinct subcellular localizations of the two isoforms result in differences in their involvement in specific processes. RalB, in particular, plays a more prominent role in apoptosis and cell motility. Additionally, RalB interacts with Exo84 to assemble the beclin-1–VPS34 autophagy initiation complex, which is critical for autophagy. It also interacts with Sec5 to activate the innate immune response via Tank-binding kinase 1 (TBK1). Clinical Significance Ral proteins, including RalB, are associated with the progression of various cancers, such as bladder cancer and prostate cancer. Although the precise mechanisms remain unclear, research indicates that RalB promotes tumor invasion and metastasis. Inhibiting RalB has been shown to suppress cancer progression. Furthermore, RalB regulates p53 levels in a manner independent of K-Ras during cancer development. RalB also enhances cell survival during infections by double-stranded DNA viruses by activating TBK1, which mediates an immune response. Interactions RalB has been demonstrated to interact with several proteins, including: CDC42, a small GTPase involved in cell signaling, EXOC8, a component of the exocyst complex, RALBP1, a Ral-binding protein involved in endocytosis and transport, and Sec5, another component of the exocyst complex that participates in immune signaling and vesicle trafficking.
